unit.title: Assemble & disassemble scaffolding to enable access to the work area

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name of the flat steel plate fitted at the foot of each standard?
A scissor lift is one kind of powered access platform. By what four-letter abbreviation are these machines usually known?
What name is given to the way of fitting a tower's guardrails in which the worker stays sitting in the platform opening, below the new level?
What is the one-word name for the space between two pairs of standards along the length of a scaffold?
Which tool is used to check that a scaffold platform or ledger is level?
What name is given to a guardrail set that is fitted from the level below, before a worker steps onto the new platform?
What is the name of the strap, often with a shock absorber, that joins a worker's harness to the anchor point?
What name is given to a scaffold built from ready-made frames with the uprights and cross-pieces welded together, rather than from loose tubes and couplers?
A tower maker's instructions give a height-to-least-base ratio of 3 to 1 for outdoor use. The tower's narrowest base side is 1.45 m. What is the greatest platform height allowed, in metres?
In the usual tag system, what colour shows that a scaffold has been inspected and is safe to use?
What three-word term covers any work where a person could fall a distance that could injure them?
What is the name of the long diagonal brace that runs across the front face of a scaffold, from bottom to top?
What is the name of the timber or metal plank laid on the transoms to make the working platform?
A platform will carry two workers of 90 kg each and 70 kg of tools and cable. What is the total load, in kilograms?
What is the name for the secure fixing point that a harness lanyard or a scaffold tie is attached to?

essays.stem: You must install cable tray and lighting along a 30 m warehouse wall at 6 m high. Explain how you would choose between a mobile tower, a fixed scaffold and other access, and what you would plan before work starts.
essays.modelAnswer: I would visit the site and look at the floor (firm, level, any slopes or drains), the height, the space along the wall, obstructions such as racking and machines, overhead lines or live equipment, and who else works there. For a long run at 6 m on a good floor, a mobile tower that can be moved along the wall is usually best, because work lasts days and needs a guarded platform for tools and tray. If the floor is poor, the run is very high or the area is busy, a fixed scaffold may be better. A powered access platform could be used if the team is trained for it. Ladders would only suit short, light tasks. I would then plan the work: a risk assessment and method statement, the tower type and the maker's instructions, the trained people who will erect it, the inspection and tagging, how materials get up, the exclusion zone below, the weather, a rescue plan, and a briefing for the team.
markingPoints: Surveys the floor, height, space, obstructions, electrical hazards and people
Compares mobile tower, fixed scaffold and other access, with reasons
Chooses suitable access for this job
Plans risk assessment, method statement, maker's instructions and trained erectors
Plans inspection, materials, exclusion zone, weather, rescue and briefing

essays.stem: Your crew will use a mobile tower to rewire the lighting in a church hall. Describe, in order, how the trained members put the tower up to the maker's instructions, and how it is checked before the electricians use it.
essays.modelAnswer: The team reads the maker's instructions and checks the height planned is allowed for the base size and whether outriggers are needed. The area is barriered and the ground checked to be firm and level, with no overhead hazards. All parts are laid out and checked: frames for bends, cracks and damaged spigots, braces with working hooks, boards with good locks, castors with working brakes. The base is built with the castors locked and levelled with the adjustable legs. Frames and braces are added in the order the maker gives, checking level and square as the team goes, with outriggers fitted where needed. Platforms are fitted, and guardrails at each level are put in from a safe position, using advance guardrails or the through-the-trap method, before anyone stands up on that level. Toe boards go on the working platform. When it is complete, a competent person inspects it, records the check and fixes a green tag, and only then is it handed over for use.
markingPoints: Reads the maker's instructions; checks height, base and outriggers
Barriers the area and checks ground and overhead hazards
Inspects all parts before use
Builds in the maker's order, castors locked, levelled, guardrails fitted from a safe position
Toe boards fitted; inspected, recorded and tagged before handover

essays.stem: Describe the main parts of a tube-and-fitting access scaffold and the job each part does.
essays.modelAnswer: Sole boards are timbers laid on the ground to spread the load over soft ground, and base plates sit on them under each standard. Standards are the upright tubes that carry the load down to the ground. Ledgers run horizontally along the length of the scaffold, joining the standards and supporting the transoms. Transoms span from front to back and carry the boards. Braces run diagonally, along the face and across the scaffold, to stop it swaying and keep it square. Ties fix the scaffold to the building so it cannot fall towards or away from it. Couplers join the tubes: right-angle couplers at 90°, swivel couplers at any angle, putlog couplers for transoms, and sleeve couplers or joint pins for joining tubes end to end. Scaffold boards make the working platform. Guardrails (top and middle rails) and toe boards stop people and materials falling from the platform, and a ladder or stair gives safe access.
markingPoints: Sole boards and base plates spread the load
Standards carry load; ledgers and transoms support the platform
Braces stop sway; ties hold it to the building
Couplers named with their uses
Boards, guardrails, toe boards and access ladder described

essays.stem: Explain how a scaffold is inspected before use and at intervals, what the inspector looks for, and how the tag system works.
essays.modelAnswer: A competent person inspects the scaffold after it is erected and before it is first used, then at the intervals the Centre's rules or the site set, and again after any change, damage, strong wind or heavy rain. Users also look it over each day before climbing. The inspector checks the base (firm ground, sole boards, base plates, castors locked), that standards are plumb and ledgers level, that braces and ties are in place and couplers are tight, that boards are sound, fully supported and not overhanging too far, that top rails, mid rails and toe boards are fitted wherever a person could fall, that the ladder is secure, and that the load and the area below are under control. Each check is written in the register. A tag at the access point shows the status: a green tag means it has been inspected and is safe to use, with the date and the inspector's name, while a red tag means do not use. Only the competent person changes a tag.
markingPoints: Inspected by a competent person before first use, at intervals and after changes or bad weather
Users check daily before climbing
Lists what is checked: base, plumb and level, braces, ties, couplers, boards, guardrails, access, loads
Results recorded in a register
Tag system: green safe with date and name, red do not use; only the competent person changes it

essays.stem: After a lighting job in a school hall, explain how the tower is taken down safely, and what happens to each part before it goes back into the store.
essays.modelAnswer: Dismantling is planned like erecting and done only by trained people. The area below is barriered, the tag is turned to 'Do not use', and all tools and materials are cleared off the platforms. The scaffold is taken down from the top, in the reverse order of erecting. Guardrails stay in place on a level until that level is being removed, so the workers are always protected, and ties and braces are not removed until the parts above them are down, so the scaffold stays stable. Parts are passed down by hand or lowered on a hand-line, never thrown. When the scaffold is down, every part is checked: tubes for bends, cracks and rust, couplers for damaged threads, frames for damaged welds and spigots, boards for splits, and castors and brakes. Good parts are cleaned and sorted by type and size. Damaged ones are labelled and put aside for repair or scrap. Everything is stored off the ground, under cover and in racks, ready for next use.
markingPoints: Plans, barriers the area, red-tags it and clears the platforms
Dismantles top down in reverse order
Keeps guardrails, ties and braces until parts above are removed
Lowers parts by hand or line, never thrown
Checks, sorts, quarantines damaged parts and stores off the ground, under cover

essays.stem: Explain the electrical hazards of using scaffolds and towers on electrical jobs, including overhead lines and work near live equipment, and how each is controlled.
essays.modelAnswer: Scaffold tubes and aluminium towers conduct electricity. If a tube or a tower touches or comes close to an overhead line, everyone touching the scaffold can be electrocuted. The team must find any overhead lines before planning, keep well clear, never move a tower under or near a line, and get advice from the power company, which may cover or switch off the line or set a safe distance. Long tubes and conduit must be carried and passed up carefully so they do not swing towards a line. Inside buildings, a tower may stand close to distribution boards, busbars or old wiring. Before any work on or near them, the circuits must be safely isolated: switched off, locked off, tagged and proved dead with a tester that is checked before and after use. Drilling into ceilings and walls needs a cable detector and drawings to avoid hidden cables. Power tools used on the tower should be battery or 110 V, with leads kept clear of moving parts. Only the instructor or an authorised person re-energises.
markingPoints: Scaffolds and towers conduct electricity
Overhead lines: find them, keep clear, consult the power company, care with long items
Safe isolation near boards or busbars: off, lock, tag, prove dead with a checked tester
Hidden cables: drawings and cable detector before drilling
Safe tools and leads on the tower; only authorised persons re-energise

essays.stem: Explain how you would protect the public and other workers below a tower that is being used to fit floodlights in a busy shopping plaza car park.
essays.modelAnswer: I would plan the work with the plaza manager so it is done at a quiet time, such as early morning, and so cars can be kept away from the work area. Before the tower goes up, I would set up a barriered exclusion zone around it, wide enough to catch anything that falls or bounces, with signs, and a banksman or ground person to keep people and cars out and guide any traffic. The tower would have toe boards fitted, and tools and parts would be kept in bags or boxes on the platform, with tool lanyards on drills and spanners. Floodlights and brackets would be raised with a hand-line or gin wheel, not carried up the ladder or thrown. Nothing would be left loose on the platform at breaks. If the wind gets up, work stops. At the end of each day, the tower is made safe or taken down, and the area is left clear and tidy.
markingPoints: Plans timing and traffic with the plaza management
Barriered exclusion zone with signs and a ground person
Toe boards, tool lanyards and contained materials
Safe lifting of floodlights by hand-line or gin wheel
Stops for wind; secures or removes tower and clears area each day

essays.stem: Explain how ground conditions and the weather in Jamaica, including heavy rain and the hurricane season, affect the safe use of scaffolds, and what the team leader should do.
essays.modelAnswer: Scaffolds need firm, level ground. Heavy rain can soften soil, wash out fill, and make a base sink on one side, so a scaffold that was safe yesterday can lean today. Sole boards and base plates spread the load, but after rain the base must be checked again before anyone climbs. Rain also makes boards, rungs and couplers slippery, so work should stop in heavy rain and boards should be checked for mud. Strong sun heats aluminium and makes it hard to hold, so gloves and water breaks are needed. Wind is the biggest danger to towers: they can blow over, and sheeting or banners make this worse. The team leader should follow the maker's wind limit, stop work when wind rises, and keep watch on forecasts. In the hurricane season, when a storm is coming, towers should be taken down and stored, and fixed scaffolds checked, tied and cleared of loose boards. After any storm, a competent person must inspect before use.
markingPoints: Rain softens ground and causes settlement: recheck base after rain
Rain makes surfaces slippery: stop work, check boards
Wind can overturn towers; no sheeting; follow maker's wind limit
Hurricane season: watch forecasts, dismantle or secure before a storm
Inspection by a competent person after storms; heat precautions

essays.stem: Explain how falls from scaffolds are prevented, and when a harness is needed. Include how a harness is checked and why a rescue plan is required.
essays.modelAnswer: The first aim is to stop a fall happening at all. Scaffolds and towers must be built by trained people to the maker's instructions, with full boarded platforms, top rails, mid rails and toe boards wherever a person could fall, safe access by a ladder or stairs, and guardrails fitted from a safe position as the tower goes up. Nobody climbs the outside or stands on rails, boxes or steps on the platform. A harness is needed where the Centre's rules, the maker or the method statement require it, for example where edge protection cannot be fitted or while some scaffold parts are being put up or taken down. It must be clipped to a proper anchor point, not to a guardrail that is not rated for it. Before use, the harness and lanyard are checked for cuts, worn stitching, damaged buckles and hooks, and an in-date inspection label. Because a person hanging in a harness can quickly come to harm, a rescue plan with trained people and equipment must be ready before work starts.
markingPoints: Prevention first: built by trained people, full platforms, guardrails and toe boards
Safe access and no climbing outside or standing on rails
Harness where rules, maker or method statement require, clipped to a proper anchor
Harness and lanyard checks before use
Rescue plan needed because suspension quickly harms

essays.stem: As team leader, explain how you would brief and supervise a team of four who will erect, use and take down a tower over three days.
essays.modelAnswer: Before work starts I would check that the people who will erect and dismantle the tower are trained and authorised, and that the tower, harnesses and tools have been inspected. I would brief the whole team using the risk assessment and method statement: the job, the tower and the maker's instructions, who does what, the exclusion zone, the electrical hazards and the isolation needed, the PPE, the weather limits, how materials go up, and the rescue plan. I would make sure everyone knows they can stop the work if something looks unsafe. During erection I would watch that the maker's order is followed and that guardrails go on before anyone stands on a level. I would have the tower inspected and tagged before use, check it each morning and after rain or wind, and record the checks. During the work I would check that brakes stay locked, that nobody overloads the platform or moves the tower while it is occupied, and that tools are tied. At the end, I would supervise the dismantling and the storage of parts, and report any damage.
markingPoints: Checks training, authorisation and equipment before starting
Full briefing from risk assessment and method statement, with roles and right to stop
Supervises erection in the maker's order and guardrail fitting
Arranges inspection, tagging, daily checks and records
Monitors safe use, then supervises dismantling, storage and reporting

practical1.title: Plan, erect, inspect and use a mobile tower for a high-level electrical task
practical1.brief: The task is to fix two cable tray brackets and a light fitting (none connected to any supply) to the training ceiling frame in the Centre's high bay. Work only under the direct supervision of the instructor, who is trained and authorised to erect towers. As a team: (1) write a short risk assessment and method statement, including the exclusion zone and a rescue plan; (2) read the maker's instructions and work out the allowed platform height for the base size; (3) lay out and check every part of the tower, and set aside any damaged part; (4) erect the tower in the maker's order, with castors locked, level, outriggers fitted if the maker requires, and guardrails fitted from a safe position at each level; (5) inspect it with the instructor using a checklist, and only use it when the instructor has passed and tagged it; (6) take turns on the platform, one at a time with tools on lanyards, to fix a bracket or the fitting while the others keep the zone and pass materials up on a hand-line; (7) take the tower down in reverse order and store the parts. Every member erects part of the tower, works on the platform and acts as ground person. Photograph each stage.
materials: Mobile aluminium tower with the maker's instructions, outriggers and toe boards
Two cable tray brackets, a light fitting and fixings (not connected to any supply)
Hand-line and bag for lifting materials; tool lanyards
Barriers, signs and a spirit level
Hard hats, gloves, safety boots and harnesses where the Centre's rules require
Risk assessment, method statement and inspection checklist forms; a phone or camera
photos: The written risk assessment and method statement
All tower parts laid out and checked, with any damaged part set aside
The base built, levelled, with castors locked
Guardrails being fitted from a safe position at a level
The finished tower with toe boards, the exclusion zone and the instructor's tag
A member fixing a bracket on the platform, with tools on lanyards
The parts sorted and stored after dismantling
checklist: Helped write the risk assessment and method statement, including the rescue plan
Checked parts and set aside any that were damaged
Followed the maker's order, locked the castors and checked level
Fitted guardrails from a safe position before standing on a level
Did not climb or use the tower until it was passed and tagged
Worked safely on the platform with tools tied and kept the zone as ground person
Dismantled in reverse order and lowered parts by hand or line
safety: Only the instructor or a trained, authorised person leads the erecting and dismantling; trainees work under direct supervision
Nobody climbs until the tower is inspected and tagged; brakes stay locked and the tower is never moved with anyone on it
Wear a hard hat, gloves and safety boots; wear a harness where the Centre's rules or the maker require it
Keep the barriered exclusion zone clear; use a hand-line and tool lanyards
Nothing at the work position is connected to any supply; stop work in strong wind or if anything looks wrong

practical2.title: Inspect a scaffold with planted faults, report on it, then dismantle and store it
practical2.brief: Before the session, the instructor (trained and authorised) erects a small one-lift tube-and-fitting or frame access scaffold beside a training wall, with planted faults such as a missing toe board, a loose coupler, a base plate with no sole board on soft ground, a split board, a missing brace and an out-of-date tag. The scaffold is red-tagged, and nobody climbs it. As a team: (1) inspect the scaffold from the ground and the ladder foot with a checklist, and record every fault with its location and why it matters; (2) agree the action for each fault and tell the instructor; (3) under the instructor's direct supervision, help to correct the faults, then take part in a re-inspection; (4) plan and carry out the dismantling, top down in reverse order, lowering every part by hand; (5) check every part, sort it by type, and label any damaged part for quarantine; (6) store the parts in racks off the ground; (7) write a short inspection and dismantling report. Every member inspects part of the scaffold, takes part in the dismantling and writes part of the report. Photograph each stage.
materials: A small access scaffold erected by the instructor, with planted faults and a red tag
Scaffold inspection checklist and report forms
Scaffold spanners or the tools the system needs
Hard hats, gloves and safety boots; harnesses where the Centre's rules require
Storage racks, and a phone or camera for photos
photos: The scaffold as found, with its red tag and the barriered zone
Each planted fault, close up, with the checklist entry
The faults being corrected under supervision
Dismantling from the top, with a part being lowered by hand
The parts sorted, with damaged items labelled for quarantine
The parts stored in racks, and the finished report
checklist: Found and recorded faults accurately, with their location and the reason they matter
Proposed a correct action for each fault
Did not climb or use the scaffold until the instructor allowed it
Dismantled in the correct order, keeping guardrails until their level came down
Lowered parts by hand and never threw them
Checked parts and quarantined damaged ones with labels
Wrote a clear part of the inspection and dismantling report
safety: The scaffold is red-tagged: nobody climbs it until the instructor says so
All corrections and dismantling are done under the direct supervision of the trained instructor
Wear hard hats, gloves and safety boots; harnesses where the Centre's rules require
Keep the barriered zone clear while parts are lowered; never throw anything down
Lift long tubes and frames with two people and watch for others nearby
